treatment.educationalObjective: The viewer leaves knowing that the first shopping cart was literally a folding chair with a basket on the seat and wheels on the legs (Sylvan Goldman, Humpty Dumpty stores, 1936-37), that shoppers first rejected it, and that Goldman made it normal by having people push carts around the store.
treatment.visualHook: Frame 0: a wooden folding chair, wired basket on its seat and casters on its legs, rolls down a 1930s grocery aisle toward the camera. It is obviously a chair, and obviously being used as a cart.
mechanismsToAnimate: chair + basket on the seat + wheels on the legs = carrier (exploded assembly, orbit)
why 'folding': the seat folds up once the basket is lifted off
social proof: models push carts, then shoppers follow (store plan)
factualRisks: RESEARCH PENDING: only one fact is quote-verified on a non-Wikipedia source (Oklahoma Historical Society); channel rule needs two
L2 'shoppers first refused to push it' and L6 'pushed her last baby' are not contained in the captured quotes (see evidence report)
search summaries disagree on 1936 vs 1937 for the idea; narration follows the cited source (idea 1936, introduction 1937)

the pram comparison in S6 is an interpretation of the woman's remark (marked conceptual)

scenes.visualPurpose: Hook: an obvious folding chair, basket on the seat and wheels on its legs, rolls down a warm 1930s grocery aisle toward a low camera. The viewer sees the punchline before hearing it.
Shoppers in period silhouettes walk past carrying hand baskets; one stops beside the chair-cart, looks, and walks on. The cart is left alone in the aisle.
Origin: the timeline lands on 1936; grocer Sylvan Goldman (silhouette) watches a shopper's hand basket fill until groceries pile over the rim. The problem is the basket's size, shown, not told.

Mechanism: under a spotlight a plain folding chair turns; the basket drops onto the seat, then four wheels slide onto the legs and lift it. Each part is named as it arrives. Chair + basket + wheels = carrier.
Why 'folding basket carriers': the timeline moves to 1937 as the basket lifts off and the seat folds flat against the back, then unfolds; Goldman's own name for them appears as a verbatim quote.
The objection: a shopper stands, arms on hips, beside the carrier; on 'pushed' a dashed pram outline draws itself over the cart, making the comparison she felt (interpretation, marked conceptual).
Social proof from above: a store plan; hired models (amber) push carts along the aisles, then the shoppers (teal) start taking carts too. Paths are illustrative, not a plan of the real store.
Payoff: back in the aisle, carts multiply into a row and shoppers push them; then everything clears and the camera settles exactly where the video began, so the loop restarts on the lone chair-cart.
